content: The report titled Insights from Optifood Modeling to Support Revision of Infant and Young Child Feeding Recommendations was authored by Mary Arimond, Elaine Ferguson, and Doris Wiesmann in June 2022. The authors express their gratitude to numerous individuals who contributed advice, discussions, assistance, and data throughout the project. Key acknowledgments include: Lawrence Grummer-Strawn, Lisa Rogers (WHO), and Chessa Lutter (consultant to WHO) for their guidance and advice during the project. Members of the WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) on Feeding Infants and Young Children aged 6-23 months, particularly the subgroup on modeling, including Richmond Aryeetey, Kathryn Dewey, Lora Iannotti, Rafael Pérez-Escamilla, Inês Rugani Ribeiro de Castro, and Zhenyu Yang. Kathryn Dewey also provided initial estimates of energy requirements and amino acid content in lipid-based nutrient supplements. Seth Adu-Afarwuah for input on selecting nutrient reference values. Veronica Luque for discussions on the European Childhood Obesity Project (CHOP) study. Lital Keinan-Boker, Rebecca Goldsmith, Tal Shimony, and Lesley Nitsan for discussions on Israeli data. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified specific topics that could benefit from diet or food pattern modeling approaches to complement systematic and narrative reviews. The Optifood modeling system was selected for this purpose. Optifood uses a multi-objective optimization method called goal programming, which allows simultaneous modeling of multiple objectives, such as meeting various nutrient requirements. The system generates solutions that minimize nutrient gaps while adhering to constraints like energy intake and food group consumption limits. The modeling exercise aimed to address several questions, including whether nutrient needs can be met with unfortified best-case food patterns, the impact of eliminating food groups, the effects of monotonous staple food consumption, and the role of fortified foods or unhealthy foods in filling nutrient gaps. The starting point for these analyses was the development of feasible best-case food patterns, which were based on generous but realistic quantities of nutrient-dense food subgroups. The report also details the methods used, including the development of parameters for modeling, food group and subgroup definitions, and nutrient reference values. The modeling incorporated data from various sources, including national and sub-national surveys, unpublished reports, and previous Optifood studies. The authors emphasize that while the modeling exercise provides valuable insights, additional work is needed to develop specific food-based recommendations for different settings.
